Before the rise of Islam, the Arabian Peninsula was home to a diverse range of religions [d1][d5]. The dominant form was Arabian polytheism, based on the veneration of deities and spirits, including the chief god Hubal and goddesses al-Lāt, al-'Uzzā, and Manāt, with the Kaaba in Mecca serving as a central shrine [d1][d6]. Alongside polytheism, Christianity (in forms such as Miaphysitism and Nestorianism), Judaism, Mandaeism, and Zoroastrianism were also present in the region [d1][d5]. From the fourth century onward, monotheism became increasingly prevalent, with Jewish and Christian communities growing and a small group of followers of Abraham's monotheistic tradition also present [d1][d5][d4]. The NYT source confirms that by the sixth century C.E., the Kaaba had become the center of religious life in what Muslims call the Jahiliyyah — "the Time of Ignorance" — an era dominated by paganism [d9]. From an Islamic theological perspective, d7 adds that all prophets before Muhammad practiced "Islam" in a general sense (submission to Allah), though this is a doctrinal view distinct from the historical record.
